title: AI Can See Optical Illusions
gist: Despite the title referencing AI, the retrievable article text covers only the human 'subjective color' phenomenon (Benham's Top), explained by predictive-processing feedback in the visual cortex, with fMRI evidence backing the model; the paywall cuts off before any AI-related content appears, so no AI claims can be extracted from this text.

themes.theme: Subjective color and the predictive brain

insights.claim: Spinning a black-and-white patterned disk known as Benham's Top produces perceived colors that aren't physically present, a phenomenon called 'subjective color' first noted by researchers and turned into a toy by Charles Benham roughly 200 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Describes a long-studied but still not fully explained visual perception phenomenon; sets up the article's neuroscience discussion.
insights.quote: Spinning a white disk with a series of black lines produced colors where there weren't any. A toymaker named Charles Benham turned the optical illusion into a toy, and Benham's Top was born.

insights.claim: The leading explanation for subjective color is that it arises from feedback in the visual cortex: the brain doesn't just passively receive visual input but actively anticipates and predicts information to fill in gaps, and fMRI studies support this predictive-feedback model.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames a predictive-processing account of perception—a neuroscience framework with broader relevance to how brains construct experience from ambiguous input.
insights.quote: The best working theory for subjective color is that it comes from feedback in our visual cortex...our brains aren't just sitting there waiting, they're anticipating and predicting information to fill in the gaps.
